lessons.title: The key water quality parameters
lessons.html:
Water is the fish's whole environment

Fish live, breathe, feed and excrete in the same water. Most losses on South African fish farms trace back to poor water quality, not to disease alone. As a supervisor you must know what each parameter means, how they interact and what to do when one goes out of range.

Dissolved oxygen (DO)

Fish take oxygen from the water through their gills. Warm water holds less oxygen than cold water, and fish need more oxygen when they are warm, feeding or stressed. DO is usually lowest just before sunrise in ponds, because algae use oxygen at night. Trout need clearly higher oxygen levels than tilapia or catfish. Use the target range set in your farm's procedures for each species.

Temperature

Temperature controls metabolism, appetite and growth. Tilapia and catfish are warm-water species and slow down sharply in a Highveld winter. Trout are cold-water fish and suffer when summer water warms. Sudden changes stress fish more than slow seasonal change.

pH

pH measures how acid or alkaline the water is. In ponds it rises in the afternoon as algae use carbon dioxide and falls overnight. Extreme or fast-changing pH damages gills.

Ammonia and nitrite

Fish excrete ammonia through their gills, and uneaten feed breaks down into ammonia too. The un-ionised form of ammonia is the toxic one, and its share rises as pH and temperature rise. Bacteria convert ammonia to nitrite, which is also toxic, and then to nitrate, which is far less harmful. In recirculating systems the biofilter does this work.

Other parameters

  • Alkalinity and hardness buffer pH swings; low-alkalinity water swings badly.
  • Carbon dioxide builds up in dense systems and makes it harder for fish to use oxygen.
  • Turbidity and suspended solids irritate gills and block filters.
  • Salinity matters for marine species and some treatments.

lessons.title: Monitoring and recording water quality
lessons.html:
A monitoring routine

Water quality changes over hours, so one reading a week is useless. Set a routine and keep to it.

ParameterTypical timingTool
DO and temperatureAt least dawn and afternoon, more in summer or high densityDO meter
pHDaily or as the procedure sayspH meter or test kit
Ammonia, nitriteSeveral times a week, daily in recirculating systemsTest kit or photometer
Alkalinity, hardnessWeekly or monthlyTest kit

Good measuring practice

  • Calibrate meters as the manufacturer instructs. An uncalibrated DO meter gives false comfort.
  • Measure at the same spot and depth each time, away from aerators and inflows.
  • Rinse probes and sample bottles between units to avoid cross-contamination.
  • Check the expiry dates of test kit reagents.

Recording and trends

Record each reading with date, time, unit and the name of the person. Plot readings over time. A slow fall in dawn oxygen over a week, or a steady rise in ammonia, warns you before fish die. Link water records to feeding records: when ammonia rises, check whether feed rates went up or fish stopped eating.

Reading fish behaviour

Fish are living indicators. Gasping at the surface, crowding at the inflow, flared gills, lethargy and loss of appetite all point to water problems. Never rely on behaviour alone; confirm with a measurement.

Water source and the law

Know where your water comes from: borehole, river, dam or municipal supply. Borehole water may be low in oxygen and high in carbon dioxide or iron. River water carries silt, pollution and wild fish diseases. Taking and using water, and discharging used water, are regulated under the National Water Act 36 of 1998, so the farm must comply with its water use authorisation.

lessons.title: Correcting water quality problems
lessons.html:
Act fast, then find the cause

When a reading goes out of range, first protect the fish, then find out why.

Low oxygen

  1. Stop feeding at once; digestion raises oxygen demand.
  2. Start backup aerators, paddlewheels or oxygen supply.
  3. Increase water exchange if clean water is available.
  4. Check for causes: aerator failure, power cut, algal bloom crash, overstocking, hot still weather.

High ammonia or nitrite

  • Reduce or stop feeding.
  • Increase water exchange.
  • In recirculating systems check the biofilter: flow, oxygen in the filter, and whether a recent chemical treatment harmed the bacteria.
  • Avoid raising pH while ammonia is high, because more ammonia becomes toxic.
  • Remove dead fish and uneaten feed.

pH and alkalinity

Agricultural lime is often used in earth ponds to raise alkalinity and stabilise pH. Apply only at rates set by the manager or a specialist. Wear eye protection, gloves and a dust mask when handling lime.

Algal blooms

Some algae are useful: they produce oxygen and natural food. A very thick bloom can crash suddenly, and as it rots, oxygen collapses. Watch water colour and transparency. Reduce fertilising and feeding and increase exchange when blooms get too dense.

Prevention

  • Stock to the planned density.
  • Feed to appetite and avoid waste.
  • Maintain aerators, pumps and generators, and test backup power regularly.
  • Keep inflow screens clean and protect the water source.

Supervising the team

Train workers to take readings correctly and to report out-of-range values immediately. Post the target ranges and emergency steps at each unit. Review records daily.

Key points

  • Oxygen is usually lowest at dawn and in hot weather.
  • Toxic ammonia increases as pH and temperature rise.
  • Calibrate meters and record readings with time and unit.
  • For low oxygen: stop feeding, aerate, exchange water, find the cause.
  • Prevention through correct stocking, feeding and maintenance is cheaper than rescue.
